extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Office examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) involved in §103 obviousness determinations and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and rebutting prima facie obviousness rejections during patent examination, including how to weigh prior art, rebuttal evidence, and argument. Covers standards for enablement, nexus, commensurateness, teaching away, hindsight, obvious-to-try, and related doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: References must be enabling to support an obviousness conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A conclusion of obviousness requires that the reference(s) relied upon be enabling in that it put the public in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making a claimed compound at the time the invention was made, the compound may not be legally concluded obvious. (In re Hoeksema, 399 F.2d 269, 274, 158 USPQ 596, 601 (CCPA 1968)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a method for making a claimed compound can overcome obviousness presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of a known or obvious process for making the claimed compounds overcomes a presumption that the compounds are obvious based on close structural relationships to prior art compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure of the prior art to disclose or render obvious a method for making any composition of matter (compound or mixture) precludes a conclusion that the composition would have been obvious. (In re Hoeksema; In re Grose).

rubrics_metrics.name: Once PTO makes a prima facie case, applicant bears burden to present contrary enabling evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness is made by the PTO through citation of references, the burden is on the applicant to produce contrary evidence establishing that the relied-on reference would not enable a skilled artisan to produce the claimed compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must submit evidence (declarations, data) showing the reference is not enabling for the claimed invention. (In re Hoeksema; Ashland Oil v. Delta Resins & Refractories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant must establish a nexus between proffered evidence and the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: To be entitled to substantial weight, the applicant should establish a nexus between the rebuttal evidence and the claimed invention; objective evidence of nonobviousness must be attributable to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO relies on the applicant to provide hard evidence of, e.g., commercial success; applicant bears burden of establishing that sales or other secondary considerations are tied to the claimed invention. (In re Huang; GPAC; In re Paulsen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The proffered evidence must be reasonably commensurate in scope with the claimed invention; evidence that is not commensurate may be insufficient to rebut a prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence need not show unexpected results over the entire range of properties; a showing for a single member or a narrow portion can suffice if a skilled artisan could ascertain a trend allowing reasonable extrapolation. Cases: In re Kulling; In re Grasselli; In re Chupp; In re Clemens; In re Lindner; In re Albrecht; In re Soni (procedural limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected results can rebut prima facie obviousness but are evaluated case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: A showing of unexpected superior properties may be sufficient to overcome a prima facie case of obviousness, but whether it suffices depends on the scope of claims, whether the showing is representative, and other motivations in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single exemplary showing may suffice when it establishes reasonable correlation to the claim scope (Chupp, Clemens); but unexpected properties for one species may be insufficient for a broad subgenus in some contexts (Grasselli, Greenfield, Lindner, Dillon, Albrecht). Each case evaluated on totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office personnel must weigh proffered evidence and should avoid giving evidence no weight except in rare circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering rebuttal evidence and arguments, Office personnel should weigh the proffered evidence and avoid discounting evidence entirely except rarely; they must consider timely presented evidence on the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is deemed insufficient, examiners should specifically set forth facts and reasoning that justify the conclusion. See MPEP §716 - §716.10 for evaluation of rebuttal evidence submitted under 37 CFR 1.132.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney argument is not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney argument cannot take the place of factual evidence in the record and is not evidence unless it is an admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney statements that assert what seems to follow from common experience are argument, not the kind of factual evidence required to rebut a prima facie case; must be supported by an affidavit/declaration if relied upon. See MPEP §2129, §2144.03, §716.01(c); In re Schulze; In re Geisler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of additional advantages or latent properties in prior art does not render an invention nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely recognizing latent properties or additional advantages present in the prior art does not make an otherwise known invention nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granting a patent on discovery of an unknown but inherent function would remove public domain content; recitation of an additional advantage that flows naturally from following prior art does not confer patentability. (In re Wiseman; Ex parte Obiaya; Lantech v. Kaufman; In re Lintner; In re Dillon). See MPEP §716.02 - §716.02(g) for declaratory evidence discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness test focuses on combined teachings, not physical combinability
rubrics_metrics.description: The test for obviousness is what the combined teachings of references would have suggested to those of ordinary skill in the art, not whether features of references could be bodily incorporated into one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary that inventions of references be physically combinable. However, a proposed combination cannot change the principle of operation of the primary reference or render it inoperable for its intended purpose. (In re Keller; In re Sneed; In re Nievelt; see MPEP §2143.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references only individually when rejection is based on combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: One cannot establish nonobviousness merely by attacking the references individually where the examiner's rejection is based on a combination of references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacking each reference separately does not address the combined teachings that support a §103 rejection. (In re Keller; In re Merck & Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references combined is not dispositive against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a large number of references in an obviousness rejection does not, without more, weigh against a finding of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even a detailed claim has been affirmed as obvious based on many references (e.g., thirteen references in In re Gorman). The quantity alone is not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation: limitations from specification are not to be read into the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations appearing only in the specification should not be imported into the claims unless clearly required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are not limited by the specification's examples or uses if such limitations are not recited in the claim language. (In re Van Geuns; Constant v. AMD; Ex parte McCullough). See MPEP §§2111-2116.01 for claim interpretation law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic infeasibility of a combination does not preclude a finding of obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: That a combination would not be made by businessmen for economic reasons does not mean a person of ordinary skill in the art would not make the combination for technological reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business/economic reasons alone do not show nonobviousness where technical motivation exists. (In re Farrenkopf).

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of references is not persuasive absent evidence the art tried and failed
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere age of prior art references is not persuasive of unobviousness unless there is evidence that despite knowledge of the references the art tried and failed to solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Old patents can be properly relied upon in a combination rejection (In re Wright); delay between patents is not dispositive (Ex parte Meyer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must be analogous to be relied upon; see MPEP for specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference is analogous art is a relevant determination for obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2141.01(a) and related case law for guidance on analogous art determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against impermissible hindsight in obviousness reconstructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconstruction or hindsight is permissible only to the extent it relies on knowledge within the level of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention and not on knowledge gleaned only from the applicant's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An obviousness judgment is necessarily a reconstruction, but must not include applicant-only knowledge. (In re McLaughlin). See MPEP §2141 and §2143 for establishing prima facie obviousness without hindsight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious-to-try rationale may support obviousness only in certain circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'obvious to try' rationale may support a conclusion of obviousness where one skilled in the art is choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success; it is not the standard in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obvious-to-try is appropriate when known options are finite and predictable (KSR). It is improper where the prior art gives no indication which parameters are critical or where one is exploring a new technology with only general guidance (In re O'Farrell). See KSR and In re O'Farrell.

rubrics_metrics.name: References that 'teach away' weigh against combining them
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to combine references where one or more references teach away from the claimed combination; the nature and substance of the teaching-away must be weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A teaching that criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution is significant. Mere disclosure of multiple alternatives without criticism is not a teaching away. (In re Grasselli; In re Gurley; In re Fulton). See MPEP §2141.02 and §2143.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom is evidence of nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claimed invention proceeds contrary to the accepted wisdom or conventional practice in the art, this can be evidence supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Known disadvantages that would discourage pursuit of a solution may be taken into account (In re Hedges; United States v. Adams). The totality of prior art should be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR principles apply across technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court's KSR decision and its rationales apply across technological fields and are not limited to predictable arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should not withdraw a rejection solely because the invention lies in a technology ordinarily considered unpredictable; KSR has been applied broadly (In re Kubin). See MPEP §2146 discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: When rejecting despite rebuttal evidence, state facts and reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: If the rebuttal evidence is deemed insufficient to rebut a prima facie case of obviousness, Office personnel should specifically set forth the facts and reasoning that justify this conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office must weigh evidence and articulate reasons for giving it less weight. See MPEP §716 - §716.10 and MPEP §716.01(d) for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply preponderance of the evidence standard in patentability determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard to be applied in all cases is the 'preponderance of the evidence' test: an examiner should reject a claim if, in view of the prior art and evidence of record, it is more likely than not that the claim is unpatentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §706(I) for the preponderance standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use MPEP form paragraphs when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs (e.g., MPEP §707.07(f) paragraphs 7.37–7.38) may be used where applicant's arguments are not persuasive or are moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may use standardized form paragraphs in appropriate situations, but still must consider and weigh evidence as required.
